pipeline_description: The delivered-text chain of the DICTATE path, exactly as core/daemon.py::_on_hold_end runs it, minus injection: clean_text -> disfluency filter -> voice punctuation (only when options.voice_punctuation is true). `expected` is what a HUMAN says the user must receive; it is never read back from the implementation.

semantics.must_preserve: dimension -> required reading of the OUTPUT. Scalar dimensions must be equal; set dimensions must contain every listed value (you may not lose a distinction).
semantics.must_not_acquire: dimension -> readings the output must NOT have. Catches inversion and invention, which loss-only checks miss.
semantics.must_classify_as: commands.grammar intent for the raw utterance. A sentence about a patient must be TYPED, never executed.
semantics.minimal_pair: partner case id + the one dimension the two differ in. Both members must differ in delivered text AND in that dimension's extracted reading. This is the check a per-case assertion cannot make: two outputs that are each plausible alone but identical to each other.
semantics.status: `holds` = true of shipped desktop behaviour. `known-gap` = the invariant is what SHOULD happen and the implementation does not do it yet; the runner asserts the gap still reproduces, so fixing the code turns the suite red until the case is promoted to `holds`.

cases.description: Negation is the highest-consequence distinction the pipeline can erase. No cleanup rule may drop 'not'.
cases.input: I did not take the medication
cases.expected: I did not take the medication

cases.description: The affirmative half of the negation pair.
cases.input: I took the medication
cases.expected: I took the medication

cases.description: A dose an order of magnitude apart from its pair. Number AND unit must both survive.
cases.input: give her five milligrams
cases.expected: give her five milligrams

cases.description: The 10x half of the dose pair.
cases.input: give her fifty milligrams
cases.expected: give her fifty milligrams

cases.description: Present-tense symptom report.
cases.input: the patient is in pain now
cases.expected: the patient is in pain now

cases.description: The same symptom, a different day — an entirely different clinical fact.
cases.input: the patient was in pain yesterday
cases.expected: the patient was in pain yesterday

cases.description: A committed claim.
cases.input: I am sure this happened
cases.expected: I am sure this happened

cases.description: The hedged half. In a source interview this is the difference between a quote and a libel.
cases.input: I am not sure this happened
cases.expected: I am not sure this happened

cases.description: The flagship case from the design review (issue #98): a spoken correction must not merely match desktop rollback behaviour, it must leave the CORRECTED quantity, its unit, and the marker that says which value supersedes the other — the last of which is asserted by `must_preserve_relation`, because a subset check cannot express order (#163).
cases.input: give him fifty, sorry, fifteen milligrams
cases.expected: give him fifty, sorry, fifteen milligrams

must_preserve_relation.why: `quantity` is a set dimension and `must_preserve` is a subset assertion, so {15, 50} satisfies it for this sentence AND for its inversion, which means the opposite. This pins which value wins.

cases.description: The minimal pair for `self-correction-keeps-corrected-dose`. Same words, same extracted quantity set {15, 50}, same correction marker — and the opposite instruction. It exists to prove the relation assertion has teeth: it satisfies every `must_preserve` of the flagship case, so before #163 the two were indistinguishable to this contract.
cases.input: give him fifteen, sorry, fifty milligrams
cases.expected: give him fifteen, sorry, fifty milligrams

must_preserve_relation.why: The mirror of the flagship case: here 50 is the corrected value.

cases.description: An instruction NOT to act, built from the same words as its opposite.
cases.input: do not stop the infusion
cases.expected: do not stop the infusion

cases.description: The instruction TO act. Also guards the dictate-versus-command boundary: an imperative about a patient is prose, not a YazSes command.
cases.input: stop the infusion
cases.expected: stop the infusion

cases.description: Who refused decides whose consent is on the record.
cases.input: the patient refused the transfusion
cases.expected: the patient refused the transfusion

cases.description: The same refusal, a different person.
cases.input: the caregiver refused the transfusion
cases.expected: the caregiver refused the transfusion

cases.description: The unhedged baseline its pair must not collapse into.
cases.input: she is stable
cases.expected: she is stable

cases.description: 'sort of' is a hedge of certainty; it must survive default disfluency filtering so a qualified observation is not delivered as a definite one (and not become byte-identical to its unhedged pair).
cases.input: she is sort of stable
cases.expected: she is sort of stable

cases.description: 'right' in 'not right' is the predicate of a negated assessment; default filtering must not strip it into a truncated fragment.
cases.input: that dose is not right
cases.expected: that dose is not right

cases.description: 'like' before a measurement is an approximation marker; default filtering must keep it so an estimate is not promoted to a measurement.
cases.input: the wound is like two centimetres across
cases.expected: the wound is like two centimetres across

cases.description: 'actually' marks that the second clause supersedes the first; default filtering must keep it so a correction is not delivered as a self-contradiction.
cases.input: she said no, actually she said yes
cases.expected: she said no, actually she said yes

cases.description: The same approximation marker on a time rather than a measurement — default filtering must keep 'like' so the timing does not become exact.
cases.input: he took it like an hour ago
cases.expected: he took it like an hour ago

cases.description: A self-correction trigger inside an instruction NOT to do the thing. 'delete that' is a rollback phrase, so the filter discarded everything before it and left 'branch' — an instruction against deleting became a bare noun. Losing a negation this way is worse than garbling: the surviving text reads as fluent and means the opposite. (#233)
cases.input: please do not delete that branch
cases.expected: please do not delete that branch

cases.description: The partner: the same trigger with nothing negating it really is a correction and must still roll back — and the value it rolls back to is the one that must survive. The fix for the negated case must not be 'stop rolling back'. (#233)
cases.input: give her fifty milligrams scratch that give her five milligrams
cases.expected: give her five milligrams

cases.description: Filler removal runs either side of the negation ('you know' before, 'basically' after). Stripping a filler must never take the polarity with it. `basically` itself is no longer stripped by default (#236); 'you know' is, and the negation survives both. (#233)
cases.input: you know the tests do not pass basically
cases.expected: the tests do not pass basically

cases.description: Dysfluency-Friendly Mode (opt-in): a hyphenated false start is one word spoken with difficulty, not several words. Collapsing it is the point of the mode. (#234)
cases.input: b-b-because she took fifteen milligrams
cases.expected: because she took fifteen milligrams

cases.description: The partner, and what makes the collapse pass dangerous: 'had had' and 'that that' are grammatical English, not stutters. A rule that cannot tell them apart silently rewrites the tense and the clause structure of a correct sentence — and the speaker who needs this mode is the least able to catch it. (#234)
cases.input: he said that that dose had had no effect
cases.expected: he said that that dose had had no effect

cases.description: 'never mind' is both a self-correction marker and ordinary English, and the utterance-initial guard does not reach it because the sentence has text in front: 'you should never mind the warning'. Closed by a second signal — a modal or auxiliary immediately before the trigger makes it part of the verb phrase, and a correction is an interjection that never continues the clause it interrupts. (#302)
cases.input: you should never mind the warning
cases.expected: you should never mind the warning

cases.description: 'undo' is an ordinary English verb before it is a command. A grammar that matched it anywhere would fire a keystroke instead of typing the sentence — and the count, which is the whole instruction, would be lost with it. The bare utterance stays a command; this does not. (#235)
cases.input: undo the last three commits before you deploy
cases.expected: undo the last three commits before you deploy

cases.description: 'basically' is a hedge in 'it seems basically correct' and a filler in 'basically, we rewrite it'. A filter that cannot tell them apart turns a hedge into a claim — the reader sees a confident statement the speaker never made. #146 drew this line for like/right/actually; this is the same test applied to the two words it missed. (#236)
cases.input: it seems basically correct
cases.expected: it seems basically correct

cases.description: Removing a filler must not take the sentence's punctuation with it, or leave punctuation stranded: 'this is probably fine, you know' became 'this is probably fine,' — a trailing comma typed into the document. The hedge 'probably' has to survive intact either way. (#236)
cases.input: this is probably fine, you know
cases.expected: this is probably fine

cases.description: A dose, a timeout and a time of day pass through the same filters as prose. Losing 'milligrams' leaves a bare number; losing 'pm' moves an appointment twelve hours. Neither is recoverable by reading the result. (#238)
cases.input: give her fifteen milligrams at three pm
cases.expected: give her fifteen milligrams at three pm
